case_info.scenario: A male patient in their mid-30s presented with a 4-week history of progressively increasing pain and swelling involving the bridge of their nose. Physical examination revealed a bulbous subcutaneous mass involving the upper nasal dorsum, with erythema of the overlying skin. They denied fever, chills, sweats, or recent local trauma. Computed tomography scan revealed an irregular rim-enhancing fluid collection in the soft tissues along the anterior margin of the nasal bones measuring approximately 2.1 × 2.1 × 1.4 cm, which appeared to abut the right and left nasal bones with marginal erosion (Figure 1A). Incision and drainage were performed, revealing a white cottage cheese–like discharge. An antibiotic regimen was prescribed, and the patient was discharged. At follow-up, the patient revealed that the erythema and tenderness had initially improved but then had worsened over the last few days. The patient was taken for surgical excision and debridement of the presumed nasal abscess. During the operation, the surgeons noted that the lesion possessed a capsule and was adherent to the bony/cartilaginous junction with significant scarring and bony remodeling, and a white cottage cheese–like material was expressed upon dissection of the lesion. Histological sections from the lesion showed ulcerated squamous epithelium with acute and chronic inflammation. The underlying soft tissue and bone contained numerous collections of pale eosinophilic, amorphous to fibrillary material which was surrounded by palisading histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Computed tomography (CT) image of the nasal mass displayed an irregular rim-enhancing fluid collection in the soft tissues along the anterior nasal bones (arrowhead). B, Hematoxylin-eosin (original magnification ×10) of the nasal mass showed aggregates of amorphous to fibrillary, pale eosinophilic material, surrounded by palisading histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells.
case_info.explanation: Gout is the most common form of microcrystalline arthropathy.1It is triggered by either an excessive production of uric acid or a decrease in its renal excretion.2Sustained elevation in uric acid levels leads to accumulation of mono-sodium urate crystals in various tissues and organs.2These crystals incite inflammation when ingested by neutrophils, triggering recurrent bouts of gouty arthritis, and potentially progressing to tophaceous gout over time.3 Tophus formation commonly occurs within or near joints, bursae, and tendon sheaths, often eroding bone and leading to distinctive lytic lesions.4In the head and neck region, tophi are most commonly found in the helix of the outer ear but can also rarely occur in other areas such as the middle ear, nasal bridge, nasal cavity, and larynx, leading to diverse symptoms from hearing loss to stridor.4Gouty involvement of the cricoarytenoid, temporomandibular, and sternoclavicular joints has also been documented.4 The diagnosis of gout relies on identifying negatively birefringent urate crystals in joint fluid or gouty tophus samples under a polarized light microscope (Figure 2).2Important differential diagnoses include conditions like pseudo-gout, rheumatoid nodule, and immune-mediated systemic diseases like granulomatosis with polyangiitis as they may exhibit similar otolaryngological manifestations, such as nasal bridge collapse, inflammation of the parasinus and sinuses, mucosal ulceration, among others.5 Topheous pseudogout may have remarkably similar histological findings to gout but will show rhomboid-shaped crystals with weakly positive birefringence under polarized light microscopy.6Rheumatoid nodule manifests as palisading granulomas surrounding areas of fibrinoid necrosis,7and granulomatosis with polyangiitis will present with necrotizing granulomatous inflammation without birefringent crystals. When a patient lacks a clinical history of gout or arthritic symptoms, as in the present case, the diagnosis can be particularly challenging. Typically, chronic tophaceous gout emerges following a decade or more of recurrent polyarticular gout; development of tophi without prior episodes of gouty arthritis is uncommon.8In this case, the patient did not initially disclose a history of gout, but upon further questioning during his postsurgical follow-up visit, he did report having intermittent arthritic symptoms in the past involving his fingers and toes. Surgical removal of the nasal mass was the preferred approach for this case and similar cases in the literature.2-9American College of Rheumatology guidelines also recommend that all patients diagnosed with tophaceous gout should undergo urate-lowering therapy together with a 6-month course of anti-inflammatory prophylaxis.10 The final diagnosis in this case was of a common inflammatory process that presented in an unexpected location. Tophaceous gout can be recognized or at least suspected on frozen section or routine histologic examination, but confirmatory diagnosis relies on the detection of mono-sodium urate crystals under polarized light microscopy. The clinical history of gout may be helpful but is not always readily available to the pathologist, who must maintain a high index of suspicion when confronted with an inflammatory mass-forming lesion in the head and neck.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Gout is the most common form of microcrystalline arthropathy.1It is triggered by either an excessive production of uric acid or a decrease in its renal excretion.2Sustained elevation in uric acid levels leads to accumulation of mono-sodium urate crystals in various tissues and organs.2These crystals incite inflammation when ingested by neutrophils, triggering recurrent bouts of gouty arthritis, and potentially progressing to tophaceous gout over time.3 Tophus formation commonly occurs within or near joints, bursae, and tendon sheaths, often eroding bone and leading to distinctive lytic lesions.4In the head and neck region, tophi are most commonly found in the helix of the outer ear but can also rarely occur in other areas such as the middle ear, nasal bridge, nasal cavity, and larynx, leading to diverse symptoms from hearing loss to stridor.4Gouty involvement of the cricoarytenoid, temporomandibular, and sternoclavicular joints has also been documented.4 The diagnosis of gout relies on identifying negatively birefringent urate crystals in joint fluid or gouty tophus samples under a polarized light microscope (Figure 2).2Important differential diagnoses include conditions like pseudo-gout, rheumatoid nodule, and immune-mediated systemic diseases like granulomatosis with polyangiitis as they may exhibit similar otolaryngological manifestations, such as nasal bridge collapse, inflammation of the parasinus and sinuses, mucosal ulceration, among others.5 Topheous pseudogout may have remarkably similar histological findings to gout but will show rhomboid-shaped crystals with weakly positive birefringence under polarized light microscopy.6Rheumatoid nodule manifests as palisading granulomas surrounding areas of fibrinoid necrosis,7and granulomatosis with polyangiitis will present with necrotizing granulomatous inflammation without birefringent crystals. When a patient lacks a clinical history of gout or arthritic symptoms, as in the present case, the diagnosis can be particularly challenging. Typically, chronic tophaceous gout emerges following a decade or more of recurrent polyarticular gout; development of tophi without prior episodes of gouty arthritis is uncommon.8In this case, the patient did not initially disclose a history of gout, but upon further questioning during his postsurgical follow-up visit, he did report having intermittent arthritic symptoms in the past involving his fingers and toes. Surgical removal of the nasal mass was the preferred approach for this case and similar cases in the literature.2-9American College of Rheumatology guidelines also recommend that all patients diagnosed with tophaceous gout should undergo urate-lowering therapy together with a 6-month course of anti-inflammatory prophylaxis.10 The final diagnosis in this case was of a common inflammatory process that presented in an unexpected location. Tophaceous gout can be recognized or at least suspected on frozen section or routine histologic examination, but confirmatory diagnosis relies on the detection of mono-sodium urate crystals under polarized light microscopy. The clinical history of gout may be helpful but is not always readily available to the pathologist, who must maintain a high index of suspicion when confronted with an inflammatory mass-forming lesion in the head and neck.

case_info.explanation: Gout is the most common form of microcrystalline arthropathy.1It is triggered by either an excessive production of uric acid or a decrease in its renal excretion.2Sustained elevation in uric acid levels leads to accumulation of mono-sodium urate crystals in various tissues and organs.2These crystals incite inflammation when ingested by neutrophils, triggering recurrent bouts of gouty arthritis, and potentially progressing to tophaceous gout over time.3 Tophus formation commonly occurs within or near joints, bursae, and tendon sheaths, often eroding bone and leading to distinctive lytic lesions.4In the head and neck region, tophi are most commonly found in the helix of the outer ear but can also rarely occur in other areas such as the middle ear, nasal bridge, nasal cavity, and larynx, leading to diverse symptoms from hearing loss to stridor.4Gouty involvement of the cricoarytenoid, temporomandibular, and sternoclavicular joints has also been documented.4 The diagnosis of gout relies on identifying negatively birefringent urate crystals in joint fluid or gouty tophus samples under a polarized light microscope (Figure 2).2Important differential diagnoses include conditions like pseudo-gout, rheumatoid nodule, and immune-mediated systemic diseases like granulomatosis with polyangiitis as they may exhibit similar otolaryngological manifestations, such as nasal bridge collapse, inflammation of the parasinus and sinuses, mucosal ulceration, among others.5 Topheous pseudogout may have remarkably similar histological findings to gout but will show rhomboid-shaped crystals with weakly positive birefringence under polarized light microscopy.6Rheumatoid nodule manifests as palisading granulomas surrounding areas of fibrinoid necrosis,7and granulomatosis with polyangiitis will present with necrotizing granulomatous inflammation without birefringent crystals. When a patient lacks a clinical history of gout or arthritic symptoms, as in the present case, the diagnosis can be particularly challenging. Typically, chronic tophaceous gout emerges following a decade or more of recurrent polyarticular gout; development of tophi without prior episodes of gouty arthritis is uncommon.8In this case, the patient did not initially disclose a history of gout, but upon further questioning during his postsurgical follow-up visit, he did report having intermittent arthritic symptoms in the past involving his fingers and toes. Surgical removal of the nasal mass was the preferred approach for this case and similar cases in the literature.2-9American College of Rheumatology guidelines also recommend that all patients diagnosed with tophaceous gout should undergo urate-lowering therapy together with a 6-month course of anti-inflammatory prophylaxis.10 The final diagnosis in this case was of a common inflammatory process that presented in an unexpected location. Tophaceous gout can be recognized or at least suspected on frozen section or routine histologic examination, but confirmatory diagnosis relies on the detection of mono-sodium urate crystals under polarized light microscopy. The clinical history of gout may be helpful but is not always readily available to the pathologist, who must maintain a high index of suspicion when confronted with an inflammatory mass-forming lesion in the head and neck.

case_info.explanation: Gout is the most common form of microcrystalline arthropathy.1It is triggered by either an excessive production of uric acid or a decrease in its renal excretion.2Sustained elevation in uric acid levels leads to accumulation of mono-sodium urate crystals in various tissues and organs.2These crystals incite inflammation when ingested by neutrophils, triggering recurrent bouts of gouty arthritis, and potentially progressing to tophaceous gout over time.3 Tophus formation commonly occurs within or near joints, bursae, and tendon sheaths, often eroding bone and leading to distinctive lytic lesions.4In the head and neck region, tophi are most commonly found in the helix of the outer ear but can also rarely occur in other areas such as the middle ear, nasal bridge, nasal cavity, and larynx, leading to diverse symptoms from hearing loss to stridor.4Gouty involvement of the cricoarytenoid, temporomandibular, and sternoclavicular joints has also been documented.4 The diagnosis of gout relies on identifying negatively birefringent urate crystals in joint fluid or gouty tophus samples under a polarized light microscope (Figure 2).2Important differential diagnoses include conditions like pseudo-gout, rheumatoid nodule, and immune-mediated systemic diseases like granulomatosis with polyangiitis as they may exhibit similar otolaryngological manifestations, such as nasal bridge collapse, inflammation of the parasinus and sinuses, mucosal ulceration, among others.5 Topheous pseudogout may have remarkably similar histological findings to gout but will show rhomboid-shaped crystals with weakly positive birefringence under polarized light microscopy.6Rheumatoid nodule manifests as palisading granulomas surrounding areas of fibrinoid necrosis,7and granulomatosis with polyangiitis will present with necrotizing granulomatous inflammation without birefringent crystals. When a patient lacks a clinical history of gout or arthritic symptoms, as in the present case, the diagnosis can be particularly challenging. Typically, chronic tophaceous gout emerges following a decade or more of recurrent polyarticular gout; development of tophi without prior episodes of gouty arthritis is uncommon.8In this case, the patient did not initially disclose a history of gout, but upon further questioning during his postsurgical follow-up visit, he did report having intermittent arthritic symptoms in the past involving his fingers and toes. Surgical removal of the nasal mass was the preferred approach for this case and similar cases in the literature.2-9American College of Rheumatology guidelines also recommend that all patients diagnosed with tophaceous gout should undergo urate-lowering therapy together with a 6-month course of anti-inflammatory prophylaxis.10 The final diagnosis in this case was of a common inflammatory process that presented in an unexpected location. Tophaceous gout can be recognized or at least suspected on frozen section or routine histologic examination, but confirmatory diagnosis relies on the detection of mono-sodium urate crystals under polarized light microscopy. The clinical history of gout may be helpful but is not always readily available to the pathologist, who must maintain a high index of suspicion when confronted with an inflammatory mass-forming lesion in the head and neck.

   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.

   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

Case:
A male patient in their mid-30s presented with a 4-week history of progressively increasing pain and swelling involving the bridge of their nose. Physical examination revealed a bulbous subcutaneous mass involving the upper nasal dorsum, with erythema of the overlying skin. They denied fever, chills, sweats, or recent local trauma. Computed tomography scan revealed an irregular rim-enhancing fluid collection in the soft tissues along the anterior margin of the nasal bones measuring approximately 2.1 × 2.1 × 1.4 cm, which appeared to abut the right and left nasal bones with marginal erosion (Figure 1A). Incision and drainage were performed, revealing a white cottage cheese–like discharge. An antibiotic regimen was prescribed, and the patient was discharged. At follow-up, the patient revealed that the erythema and tenderness had initially improved but then had worsened over the last few days. The patient was taken for surgical excision and debridement of the presumed nasal abscess. During the operation, the surgeons noted that the lesion possessed a capsule and was adherent to the bony/cartilaginous junction with significant scarring and bony remodeling, and a white cottage cheese–like material was expressed upon dissection of the lesion. Histological sections from the lesion showed ulcerated squamous epithelium with acute and chronic inflammation. The underlying soft tissue and bone contained numerous collections of pale eosinophilic, amorphous to fibrillary material which was surrounded by palisading histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells (Figure 1B).

case_info.explanation: Gout is the most common form of microcrystalline arthropathy.1It is triggered by either an excessive production of uric acid or a decrease in its renal excretion.2Sustained elevation in uric acid levels leads to accumulation of mono-sodium urate crystals in various tissues and organs.2These crystals incite inflammation when ingested by neutrophils, triggering recurrent bouts of gouty arthritis, and potentially progressing to tophaceous gout over time.3 Tophus formation commonly occurs within or near joints, bursae, and tendon sheaths, often eroding bone and leading to distinctive lytic lesions.4In the head and neck region, tophi are most commonly found in the helix of the outer ear but can also rarely occur in other areas such as the middle ear, nasal bridge, nasal cavity, and larynx, leading to diverse symptoms from hearing loss to stridor.4Gouty involvement of the cricoarytenoid, temporomandibular, and sternoclavicular joints has also been documented.4 The diagnosis of gout relies on identifying negatively birefringent urate crystals in joint fluid or gouty tophus samples under a polarized light microscope (Figure 2).2Important differential diagnoses include conditions like pseudo-gout, rheumatoid nodule, and immune-mediated systemic diseases like granulomatosis with polyangiitis as they may exhibit similar otolaryngological manifestations, such as nasal bridge collapse, inflammation of the parasinus and sinuses, mucosal ulceration, among others.5 Topheous pseudogout may have remarkably similar histological findings to gout but will show rhomboid-shaped crystals with weakly positive birefringence under polarized light microscopy.6Rheumatoid nodule manifests as palisading granulomas surrounding areas of fibrinoid necrosis,7and granulomatosis with polyangiitis will present with necrotizing granulomatous inflammation without birefringent crystals. When a patient lacks a clinical history of gout or arthritic symptoms, as in the present case, the diagnosis can be particularly challenging. Typically, chronic tophaceous gout emerges following a decade or more of recurrent polyarticular gout; development of tophi without prior episodes of gouty arthritis is uncommon.8In this case, the patient did not initially disclose a history of gout, but upon further questioning during his postsurgical follow-up visit, he did report having intermittent arthritic symptoms in the past involving his fingers and toes. Surgical removal of the nasal mass was the preferred approach for this case and similar cases in the literature.2-9American College of Rheumatology guidelines also recommend that all patients diagnosed with tophaceous gout should undergo urate-lowering therapy together with a 6-month course of anti-inflammatory prophylaxis.10 The final diagnosis in this case was of a common inflammatory process that presented in an unexpected location. Tophaceous gout can be recognized or at least suspected on frozen section or routine histologic examination, but confirmatory diagnosis relies on the detection of mono-sodium urate crystals under polarized light microscopy. The clinical history of gout may be helpful but is not always readily available to the pathologist, who must maintain a high index of suspicion when confronted with an inflammatory mass-forming lesion in the head and neck.

case_info.explanation: Gout is the most common form of microcrystalline arthropathy.1It is triggered by either an excessive production of uric acid or a decrease in its renal excretion.2Sustained elevation in uric acid levels leads to accumulation of mono-sodium urate crystals in various tissues and organs.2These crystals incite inflammation when ingested by neutrophils, triggering recurrent bouts of gouty arthritis, and potentially progressing to tophaceous gout over time.3 Tophus formation commonly occurs within or near joints, bursae, and tendon sheaths, often eroding bone and leading to distinctive lytic lesions.4In the head and neck region, tophi are most commonly found in the helix of the outer ear but can also rarely occur in other areas such as the middle ear, nasal bridge, nasal cavity, and larynx, leading to diverse symptoms from hearing loss to stridor.4Gouty involvement of the cricoarytenoid, temporomandibular, and sternoclavicular joints has also been documented.4 The diagnosis of gout relies on identifying negatively birefringent urate crystals in joint fluid or gouty tophus samples under a polarized light microscope (Figure 2).2Important differential diagnoses include conditions like pseudo-gout, rheumatoid nodule, and immune-mediated systemic diseases like granulomatosis with polyangiitis as they may exhibit similar otolaryngological manifestations, such as nasal bridge collapse, inflammation of the parasinus and sinuses, mucosal ulceration, among others.5 Topheous pseudogout may have remarkably similar histological findings to gout but will show rhomboid-shaped crystals with weakly positive birefringence under polarized light microscopy.6Rheumatoid nodule manifests as palisading granulomas surrounding areas of fibrinoid necrosis,7and granulomatosis with polyangiitis will present with necrotizing granulomatous inflammation without birefringent crystals. When a patient lacks a clinical history of gout or arthritic symptoms, as in the present case, the diagnosis can be particularly challenging. Typically, chronic tophaceous gout emerges following a decade or more of recurrent polyarticular gout; development of tophi without prior episodes of gouty arthritis is uncommon.8In this case, the patient did not initially disclose a history of gout, but upon further questioning during his postsurgical follow-up visit, he did report having intermittent arthritic symptoms in the past involving his fingers and toes. Surgical removal of the nasal mass was the preferred approach for this case and similar cases in the literature.2-9American College of Rheumatology guidelines also recommend that all patients diagnosed with tophaceous gout should undergo urate-lowering therapy together with a 6-month course of anti-inflammatory prophylaxis.10 The final diagnosis in this case was of a common inflammatory process that presented in an unexpected location. Tophaceous gout can be recognized or at least suspected on frozen section or routine histologic examination, but confirmatory diagnosis relies on the detection of mono-sodium urate crystals under polarized light microscopy. The clinical history of gout may be helpful but is not always readily available to the pathologist, who must maintain a high index of suspicion when confronted with an inflammatory mass-forming lesion in the head and neck.

case_info.explanation: Gout is the most common form of microcrystalline arthropathy.1It is triggered by either an excessive production of uric acid or a decrease in its renal excretion.2Sustained elevation in uric acid levels leads to accumulation of mono-sodium urate crystals in various tissues and organs.2These crystals incite inflammation when ingested by neutrophils, triggering recurrent bouts of gouty arthritis, and potentially progressing to tophaceous gout over time.3 Tophus formation commonly occurs within or near joints, bursae, and tendon sheaths, often eroding bone and leading to distinctive lytic lesions.4In the head and neck region, tophi are most commonly found in the helix of the outer ear but can also rarely occur in other areas such as the middle ear, nasal bridge, nasal cavity, and larynx, leading to diverse symptoms from hearing loss to stridor.4Gouty involvement of the cricoarytenoid, temporomandibular, and sternoclavicular joints has also been documented.4 The diagnosis of gout relies on identifying negatively birefringent urate crystals in joint fluid or gouty tophus samples under a polarized light microscope (Figure 2).2Important differential diagnoses include conditions like pseudo-gout, rheumatoid nodule, and immune-mediated systemic diseases like granulomatosis with polyangiitis as they may exhibit similar otolaryngological manifestations, such as nasal bridge collapse, inflammation of the parasinus and sinuses, mucosal ulceration, among others.5 Topheous pseudogout may have remarkably similar histological findings to gout but will show rhomboid-shaped crystals with weakly positive birefringence under polarized light microscopy.6Rheumatoid nodule manifests as palisading granulomas surrounding areas of fibrinoid necrosis,7and granulomatosis with polyangiitis will present with necrotizing granulomatous inflammation without birefringent crystals. When a patient lacks a clinical history of gout or arthritic symptoms, as in the present case, the diagnosis can be particularly challenging. Typically, chronic tophaceous gout emerges following a decade or more of recurrent polyarticular gout; development of tophi without prior episodes of gouty arthritis is uncommon.8In this case, the patient did not initially disclose a history of gout, but upon further questioning during his postsurgical follow-up visit, he did report having intermittent arthritic symptoms in the past involving his fingers and toes. Surgical removal of the nasal mass was the preferred approach for this case and similar cases in the literature.2-9American College of Rheumatology guidelines also recommend that all patients diagnosed with tophaceous gout should undergo urate-lowering therapy together with a 6-month course of anti-inflammatory prophylaxis.10 The final diagnosis in this case was of a common inflammatory process that presented in an unexpected location. Tophaceous gout can be recognized or at least suspected on frozen section or routine histologic examination, but confirmatory diagnosis relies on the detection of mono-sodium urate crystals under polarized light microscopy. The clinical history of gout may be helpful but is not always readily available to the pathologist, who must maintain a high index of suspicion when confronted with an inflammatory mass-forming lesion in the head and neck.

case_info.explanation: Gout is the most common form of microcrystalline arthropathy.1It is triggered by either an excessive production of uric acid or a decrease in its renal excretion.2Sustained elevation in uric acid levels leads to accumulation of mono-sodium urate crystals in various tissues and organs.2These crystals incite inflammation when ingested by neutrophils, triggering recurrent bouts of gouty arthritis, and potentially progressing to tophaceous gout over time.3 Tophus formation commonly occurs within or near joints, bursae, and tendon sheaths, often eroding bone and leading to distinctive lytic lesions.4In the head and neck region, tophi are most commonly found in the helix of the outer ear but can also rarely occur in other areas such as the middle ear, nasal bridge, nasal cavity, and larynx, leading to diverse symptoms from hearing loss to stridor.4Gouty involvement of the cricoarytenoid, temporomandibular, and sternoclavicular joints has also been documented.4 The diagnosis of gout relies on identifying negatively birefringent urate crystals in joint fluid or gouty tophus samples under a polarized light microscope (Figure 2).2Important differential diagnoses include conditions like pseudo-gout, rheumatoid nodule, and immune-mediated systemic diseases like granulomatosis with polyangiitis as they may exhibit similar otolaryngological manifestations, such as nasal bridge collapse, inflammation of the parasinus and sinuses, mucosal ulceration, among others.5 Topheous pseudogout may have remarkably similar histological findings to gout but will show rhomboid-shaped crystals with weakly positive birefringence under polarized light microscopy.6Rheumatoid nodule manifests as palisading granulomas surrounding areas of fibrinoid necrosis,7and granulomatosis with polyangiitis will present with necrotizing granulomatous inflammation without birefringent crystals. When a patient lacks a clinical history of gout or arthritic symptoms, as in the present case, the diagnosis can be particularly challenging. Typically, chronic tophaceous gout emerges following a decade or more of recurrent polyarticular gout; development of tophi without prior episodes of gouty arthritis is uncommon.8In this case, the patient did not initially disclose a history of gout, but upon further questioning during his postsurgical follow-up visit, he did report having intermittent arthritic symptoms in the past involving his fingers and toes. Surgical removal of the nasal mass was the preferred approach for this case and similar cases in the literature.2-9American College of Rheumatology guidelines also recommend that all patients diagnosed with tophaceous gout should undergo urate-lowering therapy together with a 6-month course of anti-inflammatory prophylaxis.10 The final diagnosis in this case was of a common inflammatory process that presented in an unexpected location. Tophaceous gout can be recognized or at least suspected on frozen section or routine histologic examination, but confirmatory diagnosis relies on the detection of mono-sodium urate crystals under polarized light microscopy. The clinical history of gout may be helpful but is not always readily available to the pathologist, who must maintain a high index of suspicion when confronted with an inflammatory mass-forming lesion in the head and neck.
